extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, engineers, academic authors and reviewers); authors of scientific/technical books
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reviewing scientific or technical books and short reports for an academic journal readership, including judgement of accuracy, pedagogy, originality, and suitability for intended audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal letter/submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by correspondents; cannot undertake to return, or to correspond with the writers of, rejected manuscripts intended for this or any other part of NATURE; no notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and correspondents should sign and accept responsibility for their letters; do not send anonymous communications; do not expect returned manuscripts or individual correspondence about rejected submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist proofreading of technical reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of technical reports/books should submit proofs for revision to competent specialists in the relevant subfield to detect domain-specific blunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to have domain experts check proofs can leave 'serious blemishes' — examples cited include incorrect identification of metallurgical processes and unintelligible descriptions of furnaces; specialist revision would catch such errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical accuracy and correct use of terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of technical processes, apparatus, and materials must be accurate and use correct terminology (e.g., correct naming of processes, correct characterization of materials like pig-iron vs malleable iron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect or contradictory statements (as in the cited Majdan furnaces passage) render descriptions unintelligible and undermine the work's value; reviewers penalize such errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution of new empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Works in largely empirical fields should present new data or evidence that confirm or modify established formulae and practice, especially where prior experimental work is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reviewer may expect the author's field experience to yield new data or comparative evidence (the hydraulics book was criticised for not adding new data despite the author's Indian irrigation experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence for methodological choices / comparative accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When adopting or favouring particular formulae or methods (e.g., Chezy vs logarithmic formula for flow), authors should present evidence or discussion of the comparative accuracy and applicability of those choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying a formula is chosen for simplicity is insufficient for serious students; comparative experimental or theoretical justification is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate treatment of difficult/important problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Important, hard problems within the subject (e.g., shape of the water surface upstream of barrages) demand fuller, more adequate treatment than a brief or perfunctory discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will mark down books that gloss over such problems or provide unsatisfactory treatment; complex topics need deeper analysis and clearer exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical development for students (pedagogical structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks intended for students should present a sufficiently logical and coherent development of fundamentals so that a student can understand the subject thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A volume that is practically oriented but lacks logical progression may be useful to practitioners but unsatisfactory for students desiring foundational understanding (criticised of the hydraulics volume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for intended audience (student vs practitioner)
rubrics_metrics.description: A book's scope, depth, style, and emphasis should match the needs of its intended audience (e.g., beginners, diploma candidates, practising engineers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assess whether the text's level and orientation fit its stated audience — e.g., radiography book praised as lucid and practical for beginners; refrigeration book targeted to engineers trained in heat-work conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization / method appropriate to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of organizational scheme should suit the book's purpose: e.g., applied entomology can be organized taxonomically (by orders) for elementary students or by crops/objects for a practical reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer recommends taxonomy-based organization for elementary teaching and crop-based layout for quick practical reference; organizational mismatch with audience is a weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and coverage of essential facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Within constrained length, a good textbook should give the essential facts and principles without unnecessary prolixity (e.g., ~400 pages giving essential biology and control of important insects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers note when an author succeeds in compressing essentials into modest length; overly abbreviated introductions may be acceptable if essentials are present, but risks exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of illustrations and production (printing), and minimal typographical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be adequate and printing of high quality; typographical errors should be few and not serious enough to detract from value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few misprints are forgivable but reviewers mention them; poor illustration quality or many errors will lower appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of up-to-date reference data and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical books should include current reference tables and data (e.g., properties of refrigerants) compiled from authoritative sources like standards bureaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of newer, more reliable tables is singled out as a strong positive feature (refrigeration book praised for Bureau of Standards tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and practical exposition of principles and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition should be lucid and practical, especially when teaching the use and construction of apparatus and basic principles (e.g., radiography: production of skiagrams, X-ray tubes, high-tension currents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lucid, practically oriented account, augmented by practical experience, enhances usefulness for beginners and practitioner-students; figures and depictions should be accurate and may be revised in later editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly/methodological rigour in textual or comparative studies
rubrics_metrics.description: In historical or textual studies (e.g., stage directions in quartos vs First Folio), rigorous comparative methodology and close textual comparison are valuable and yield useful deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodical comparison can support suggestions about stage practice and textual provenance; such deductions 'deserve attention' in resolving difficult problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design, measurement accuracy and accounting for confounding factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In experimental reports (e.g., X-ray reflection from powdered crystals), experiments should control/measure key factors (absorption/extinction) and report probable errors and comparisons with theoretical predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct measurement of absorption in powders and use of homogeneous primary rays were recommended; reviewers value quantitative comparison to theory and call for higher-accuracy results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and accurate use of source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about access to private correspondence or other source materials must be accurate; improper or undisclosed use of private letters is a serious concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accusations about who has seen private letters (as in the Ross–Sambon exchange) should be substantiated; reviewers/authors are expected to respect privacy and accurately report provenance of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient ethnographic detail when claiming anthropological value
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel or exploration narratives claiming ethnographic value should provide detailed descriptions of peoples and cultures sufficient for ethnologists to find them valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives that are vivid but skim cultural details may be entertaining for general readers but inadequate for specialists; reviewers lament lack of depth for ethnographic utility.
